title: 3. Distribution, Supply Chain & Unit Economics

epigraph.quote: We buy the important components from the technology providers and integrate them with our own designs, storage, networking and software. The finished system sells to the customer — we do not rent out GPU capacity.
epigraph.author: Synthesis of Netweb's OEM operating model, FY2026 Annual Report and Q2 FY2027 Earnings Call

web_blocks.html: Netweb's go-to-market model is a hybrid of direct enterprise selling, government and public-sector tendering, and channel-led distribution. All of it wraps around OEM partnerships with the silicon vendors. The company maintains manufacturing and R&D facilities in Delhi-NCR (Faridabad and Gurugram) and Hyderabad, with eighteen offices across India and an office in Singapore. Large sovereign and institutional orders are typically won directly through tenders or negotiated strategic contracts. Enterprise orders arrive both directly and through distributor and system-integrator partners. For example, Netweb's 2026 sovereign cyber-secure compute facility for CERT-IN was disclosed as processed through the company's distributor. Because the customer base is dominated by government, defence, research, banking and large enterprise buyers, the sales cycle is long, qualification-heavy and reference-driven.

The supply chain is the crux of the model and the crux of the risk. Netweb is an OEM, not a chipmaker. It buys GPUs from NVIDIA, CPUs from Intel and AMD, memory from Samsung, and power and cooling components from partners such as Vertiv. It then integrates them with its own chassis, board designs and software. That means its gross margin is set by the spread between component cost and the system price it can command. Its working capital is set by how long it must hold expensive components before delivery. Management has been explicit that it is deliberately carrying more inventory. Inventory days stood at 117 at September 2026 versus 86 at March 2026. The purpose is to secure critical components against longer lead times and to safeguard execution of a ₹2,629 crore order book. The flip side is equally explicit: if component prices fall or customers defer, that inventory loses value.

Pricing varies by segment. AI systems are priced per node or per rack with a service wrapper. Management has said the gross-margin profile of a very large deal is structurally different from a small one. Quarterly gross margin is therefore a function of deal mix and should not be read sequentially. HPC supercomputing projects are priced on a fixed-scope project basis plus a multi-year maintenance contract. Private cloud and HCI carry a hardware-plus-software-subscription-plus-support structure, the closest thing in the portfolio to recurring revenue. Standard execution runs 10 to 16 weeks per order. Billing on large institutional orders is milestone-and-advance based. That is why receivables improved to 62 days in Q2 FY2027 while inventory ballooned. Customers pay promptly once a milestone is met, but Netweb has already funded the components.

web_blocks.caption: Table 3.1: Netweb Technologies Audited FY2026 Revenue-to-Free-Cash-Flow Waterfall (Scaled to ₹100 Revenue)
web_blocks.takeaway: For every ₹100 of FY2026 audited revenue, ₹79.15 went into materials and inventory build, ₹13.04 covered engineering and overhead, ₹13.05 became operating EBITDA, and after interest, tax and working-capital movements, ₹7.83 arrived as free cash flow. The point of the waterfall is the gap between the ₹9.43 of accounting profit and the ₹7.83 of cash actually retained — a systems integrator's profit is earned twice, once on the income statement and again when the inventory converts.

web_blocks.html: The cash-conversion mechanics deserve particular care. They are where this business differs most from a software compounder. Receivable days were 112 in FY2026 on Screener's annualised basis and improved to 62 in Q2 FY2027. Inventory days rose to 117. The cash-conversion cycle was 94 days in Q2 FY2027 against 84 days for FY2026. Management guides the cycle to run between 90 and 110 days for the foreseeable future. Against that, customer advances on large strategic orders and the ability to stretch payables have kept the company net-debt-negative most of the time. It reported zero net debt and a small net cash position of ₹14 crore at September 2026, with roughly ₹403 crore of unutilised QIP proceeds still on the balance sheet.

web_blocks.title: Unit Economics: What a ₹100 AI Order Actually Earns
paragraphs: Strip the project accounting away and Netweb's economics per order are those of an advanced integrator. A large AI system carries roughly 13–15% operating EBITDA margin — so on a ₹100 system, the company keeps around ₹13–14 of operating profit. From that it funds engineering, R&D, sales, interest on the working-capital borrowing used to buy the components, and tax, leaving roughly ₹8–9 of bottom-line profit if collections are timely.

The critical variable is not the margin percentage; it is the time between paying the component supplier and being paid by the customer. If that gap is 90–110 days, the company must finance a full system's worth of components from its own balance sheet and its borrowings for a quarter. That is why a ₹1,200 crore equity raise was necessary even while the company reported record profits: growth, not profitability, is what consumes the cash. The unit economics work as long as order intake keeps growing and customers keep paying on schedule; they reverse sharply if either stops.

web_blocks.html: Two structural features of the distribution model are worth flagging as durable positives. First, the OEM relationships are multi-sourced and chip-agnostic. Netweb partners with NVIDIA, AMD and Intel, so it is not hostage to a single accelerator roadmap. It can adapt its designs as the market shifts between GPU and alternative architectures. Management described a two-to-three-year product roadmap and the ability to re-schematic quickly if component supply shifts. Second, the company's qualification under the PLI 1.0 and 2.0 schemes gives it a structural cost and eligibility advantage. It is one of the few Indian OEMs manufacturing IT hardware at scale. On government and sovereign tenders where local manufacturing is mandated, the customer often cannot legally or politically award the contract to an importer. That eligibility is the distribution moat.

book_paragraphs: Let us follow one rupee of Netweb revenue from the customer's purchase order all the way to free cash flow, because the journey tells you more about this company than any margin ratio. The order arrives, usually after a long qualification — a government tender, a defence procurement, a bank's technology committee, or a hyperscaler's engineering review. Netweb wins the contract on integration capability, made-in-India eligibility and price. Then comes the part that shapes the whole business: before it can deliver anything, it must buy the GPUs, the memory, the CPUs and the cooling from its partners, and it must pay for them long before the customer pays Netweb.

Picture the supply chain as a physical chain with Netweb in the middle. On one side are the technology vendors — NVIDIA for accelerators, Intel and AMD for CPUs, Samsung for memory, Vertiv for power and cooling. Netweb buys their components and adds its own chassis design, board design, storage, networking and software. On the other side is the customer, who wants a working system, not a pile of parts. Netweb's gross margin is simply the spread between what the components cost and what the integrated system fetches; its cash flow is simply how long it must hold those components before the customer's payment arrives.

Now read Table 3.1, the ₹100 waterfall, and notice how much of each hundred rupees is consumed before anything is earned. Roughly ₹79 goes to materials and the deliberate inventory build, ₹13 to engineering and overhead, leaving about ₹13 of operating EBITDA. After interest — the company was carrying ₹333 crore of borrowings at September 2026, largely to fund that inventory — after tax and depreciation, and after the working-capital movement, about ₹8 survives as free cash flow. That is a healthy number, and it is also a fragile one, because it depends on the time gap between paying suppliers and being paid.

This is why you should watch the cash-conversion cycle as closely as the profit line. At September 2026 it was 94 days, with receivables an impressive 62 days but inventory a heavy 117 days. Ask yourself why a company whose customers pay promptly is nonetheless borrowing ₹333 crore. The answer is that the company chooses to hold components against a ₹2,629 crore order book, because in a supply-constrained GPU market, being caught without inventory means missing a delivery and losing the next order. Management describes the inventory as deliberate; a sceptic would call it a bet. Both descriptions are true, and the difference only becomes visible if demand slows.

Distribution here is not the glamorous kind. There is no consumer brand and no viral product. Instead there is a factory in Faridabad, eighteen offices across India, an office in Singapore, a distributor channel for some orders, and a set of OEM partnerships that took years to earn. The distribution moat is the qualification itself: Netweb's PLI certification, its status as one of the few Indian OEMs manufacturing at scale, and its provenance on national supercomputing projects mean that on many large sovereign tenders it is one of a very small number of bidders who can even qualify. On those contracts, the competition is thin.

The chip-agnostic partnership structure is the quiet strength of the distribution model. Because Netweb builds on NVIDIA, AMD and Intel platforms, it is not locked to a single accelerator roadmap, and management has said it can re-schematic its designs within a two-to-three-year horizon as supply shifts. That flexibility is worth real money in a market where the leading chip changes every eighteen months. But it is also a reminder that Netweb's technology is, ultimately, its partners' technology — its own contribution is integration, manufacturing and support, and those are competitive but not exclusive.

So when you size this business, hold two truths together. The unit economics are genuinely attractive for an integrator: ₹13–14 of operating profit on every ₹100 sold, improving with scale. And the cash economics are genuinely demanding: growth, not profit, is what eats the balance sheet. Every rupee of revenue growth pulls more cash into inventory before it returns as cash from operations. That is exactly why the ₹1,200 crore raise happened in the same quarter as record profits, and it is the pattern you must keep watching in every future quarter.

Let me make the cash lesson concrete with a simple question you can ask of any fast-growing hardware company. If the company stopped growing tomorrow, would it generate a lot of cash or a little? For Netweb the honest answer is a lot, because a freeze on new orders would let the inventory liquidate, receivables convert and borrowings unwind. That is a comforting answer, and it is also the trap. A business that only generates cash when it stops growing is a business whose growth you must finance, and whose stall you must survive. Netweb is not fragile — it earns good margins, its customers are creditworthy and its balance sheet is now well funded. But it is a business that rewards a shareholder who understands the financing as clearly as the engineering. That understanding is exactly what this chapter is for.

book_callouts.title: Why Growth Consumes Cash Here
book_callouts.text: In a software business, growth produces cash because an extra customer costs almost nothing to serve. In Netweb's business, growth consumes cash because every extra rupee of revenue must first be spent on components. A company growing revenue 90% a year can be profitable and still need fresh capital, and that is not a red flag by itself — it is the arithmetic of a physical integrator. The red flag would be if the growth stopped while the inventory stayed on the books.
